ABB Migration.notes:
# v8

Until now this tool decoded the project and stopped. Everything it wrote was
ABB's facts, tidied — correct, useful, and still in the source system's
vocabulary. That leaves both of its users one step short: the engineer migrating
to DeltaV had nothing DeltaV-shaped to work from, and the engineer who has never
used Freelance **could not see the logic at all** — `logic_connections.csv` is a
netlist, and `B-CT-713.3` means nothing without Freelance open next to it.

## Read the logic without Freelance

**The FBD sheets are now drawn.** Every coordinate was already in the export and
nothing was rendering them. `extracted_svg/logic/` holds one SVG per sheet plus a
contact sheet: blocks that carry a plant tag — the ones that become DeltaV
modules — are drawn heavier, wires and junctions are drawn exactly as the export
has them, signals entering and leaving the sheet are named, inverted pins get
their bubble, and hovering any block gives you its tag.

**`extracted_system/block_inventory.csv`** says what each block type *is*, in one
line, and — the useful part — whether it becomes a DeltaV module or folds into
somebody else's expression. `M_ANA` is an analog measurement and becomes an
`_AI_V01`; `AND` is logic and becomes a term inside a module, not a module of its
own. Getting that distinction wrong inflates a module count, and an estimate, by
an order of magnitude. Block types the legend does not cover are listed too,
ranked by instance count, so the gaps rank themselves — and adding one to
`freelance_refdata/block_library.json` needs no code change.

**Pin names** resolve where the export publishes them (the project's own function
blocks: `PUMP_FB.START`) and read as `#3` where it does not. The index convention
for standard-library blocks has never been confirmed against a real project, so a
bare number is never dressed up as a name; those pins are documented in the block
inventory instead.

## Restated for DeltaV

- **`proposed_modules.csv`** — what each tagged block should become: the PCSD
  `MODULE_CLASS`, the evidence, and the device parameters already recovered. Two
  independent signals are used — the ABB block class, and the type of IO channel
  the tag is wired to. When they agree the row is `confirmed`; when they disagree
  it is `conflict` and gets looked at rather than averaged; when neither fires it
  is a work item naming the block type to add, not a silent gap.
- **`controller_sizing.csv`** — per source controller: tags, modules, IO by type,
  cross-controller signals, fastest scan rate. The first-cut answer to how many
  DeltaV controllers this needs.
- **`peer_to_peer.csv`** — every signal used outside its owning controller, and
  what DeltaV needs in its place.
- **Scan rates are now legal.** DeltaV accepts a discrete set of module periods
  and 0.25 s is not one of them — a 250 ms Freelance task is the common case and
  would have failed on import. `deltav_scan_ms` snaps to the nearest accepted
  period, rounding **down**, so a loop never ends up running slower than the
  plant was tuned for.
- **`io_list.csv`** gained the target side: the DeltaV card / CHARM type per
  channel. Unrecognised modules are left blank — an IO list with a wrong card
  type is worse than one with a gap.

## Proving it is complete

- **`extracted_system/coverage.csv`** — every record type in the export and
  whether this tool decoded it. The parser used to end in *"all other tags fall
  through silently"*, which meant it could not tell you what it had missed;
  "lossless" was a claim rather than a measurement.
- **`alarm_list.csv`** — one row per configured alarm instead of sixteen columns
  per tag, so the alarm load can be counted and sorted by priority. Discrete
  alarms carry no limit and are included anyway; counting only limits
  under-reports the load by every discrete point in the plant.
- **`index.html` is now the report** — size of the job, shape per controller,
  what the logic is made of, and a *Needs a decision* sectio

# SuperOPCWatchIt — release notes

## v3

**Standalone OPC-DA — nothing to install, no "Class not registered".**

- Replaced the OpenOPC + `OPC.Automation` wrapper stack with a vendored native
  32-bit helper (`opcda-bridge.exe`) that talks the OPC-DA custom interfaces
  directly. The tool no longer needs any OPC automation wrapper (Graybox /
  Matrikon / `gbda_aut.dll`) or any COM registration — the only requirement is
  the OPC server itself (e.g. `OPC.DeltaV.1`), which is already present on a
  DeltaV node.
- Fixes the "Connection error / Dispatch: Class not registered" failure, which
  was caused by the missing automation-wrapper COM class.
- Clearer connection errors: the status line now reports the actual OPC/COM
  reason (e.g. server ProgID not registered, item not writeable, unknown item).

*Note:* runs on the DeltaV node itself (local COM). Connecting to a remote
node's OPC server over DCOM is not enabled in this build.

## v2

- Advanced OPC-DA tag monitor: live browsing, CSV import/export, write audit log.

DifFHX.notes:
## v9

- Fixed very large FHX files appearing to hang while loading. The step that learns how
  to name elements uniquely searched every combination of up to five attributes, which
  on a wide export ran to hundreds of millions of attempts and never completed. Because
  DifFHX learns one naming rule across both files being compared, it was more exposed to
  this than the single-file tools. Files that previously would not load now finish in
  seconds.

FHXport.notes:
## v26

Reference Report — it no longer dies on large exports, and it is roughly 50x faster.

- **It stops running out of memory.** The report used to copy the whole element
  tree two or three times over and then copy every module class into every one of
  its instances, so peak memory was several times the size of the export. On a big
  plant export that exhausted the machine, and the tool vanished with no error at
  all — the failure happened below Python, so there was nothing to report. It now
  reads the definitions in place instead of copying them. Measured on three real
  exports: **578 MB → 2 MB**, **897 MB → 2 MB**, **1017 MB → 0.4 MB**.
- **And it is far faster** — the same three exports went from **115s, 135s and 91s
  to 2.3s, 2.2s and 3.2s**. Every row is byte-for-byte what the old version
  produced.
- **A report bigger than a worksheet no longer fails.** Excel holds 1,048,576 rows
  per sheet, and the Unknown References tab can exceed that on a whole-plant
  export; the write used to fail at the very end, after all the work. Overflow now
  continues onto `Unknown References (2)`.
- **Expression text can no longer abort the write.** Control characters copied out
  of raw FHX are rejected by Excel; they are now stripped, and over-long values
  trimmed to what a cell can hold. This applies to every report the tool writes.
- **Aliased references now show their node.** The Referenced Node column was blank
  on every reference that went through an alias, because it was looked up in the
  I/O map instead of the module map. Direct `//MODULE` references were unaffected.

Also: **FHX files saved as UTF-8 now open.** Every report read files as UTF-16
regardless, and a UTF-8 file does not fail that — it decodes to mojibake, then
fails much later as an unreadable parse error. The encoding is now detected.
Real DeltaV exports are unaffected, byte for byte.

## v23

Excel output — from follow-up feedback on the v22 Historian Report.

- **The Historian Report leads with what identifies a row.** `MODULE_NAME` /
  `UNIT_NAME` / `NODE_NAME` and `VALUE_RECORDED` are now columns 1 and 2 on every
  sheet, ahead of the module context (area, class, type, description, controller)
  that used to sit between them.
- **Each Historian sheet is sorted** by that name column, then by `VALUE_RECORDED`,
  so every point collected on one tag reads as a contiguous, alphabetical block.
- **Bold header row and auto-sized columns** on every Excel report this tool
  writes — Historian, IO, Reference and User Log — not just the Historian one.
  Column widths are capped so a single long description can't push the rest of
  the sheet off the screen.

## v22

Historian Report — from feedback by Leonard Clark.

- **Unit modules are no longer missing.** Modules with history collection configured
  on them were silently absent from the report. On a real plant export this recovered
  10 collection points that had never appeared.
- **Controller nodes are now included too** — found while fixing the above, and a
  bigger gap: 72 more points on the same export, including controller scan-time
  loading and free memory.
- **The report is now an Excel workbook** with a sheet each for Modules, Unit Modules
  and Controller Nodes, instead of one flat CSV. Note the output file is now
  `<name>_HistorianReport.xlsx` — if you have a script picking up the `.csv` by name,
  it needs updating.
- **Column changes**, to line the report up with the standard DeltaV historian export:
  - `VALUE_RECORDED` (e.g. `LAS-36501A/PV.CV`) replaces the separate `PARAMETER`
    and `FIELD` columns
  - `TAG` is now `MODULE_NAME`, `UNIT_NAME` or `NODE_NAME`, per sheet
  - `EXPOSED` is now `ALLOW_INSTANCE_CONFIG`
  - added `MODULE_TYPE` and `MODULE_SUBTYPE`

Also in this release: Named Set Reports, and an SFC formatting fix in the EM and
Phase reports.

FHXEdit.notes:
## v8

- Fixed very large FHX exports appearing to hang after parsing. The log would report
  "Successfully parsed N top-level elements" and then go quiet, with Open Editor View,
  Split, Trim and Update Timestamps staying greyed out indefinitely. Parsing had not
  actually finished: a post-parse step that learns how to name elements uniquely was
  searching every combination of up to five attributes, which on a wide file meant
  hundreds of millions of attempts. A 331 MB customer export now loads in about 35
  seconds; previously it would not finish at all.
- The status log now reports progress through that identity-learning step, so it can
  no longer look finished while work is still running.
- Fixed unreadable text on machines with Windows dark mode enabled. The tree filter
  box, element rows in the tree, the Advanced Find/Replace window and the parse
  confirmation dialog could all render text the same colour as their background.

EMTools.notes:
# v5
Generate now works against every PCSD template, not just the command-driven one, and
performs the device fix-up that previously had to be done by hand in DeltaV.

Device references now follow the rename:
- Renaming a device slot (`DEV1` → your alias) now reaches the composites, not just
  the block declarations. MONITOR's failure roll-up, the command SFC confirm
  expressions and the ACQ_REL acquire/release statements all addressed `/DEV1/`
  directly and were left pointing at blocks that no longer existed — every generated
  EM shipped with dead device monitoring and step confirmations, at every device
  count, on every template type.
- Requesting fewer devices than a template ships now removes the surplus slots
  properly: per-device elements are deleted, structured-text statements dropped, and
  boolean clauses pruned with their connector so the expression stays balanced. A
  prune that would unbalance an expression is refused and reported instead.
- Multi-slot comment boxes (the arbitration instructions, the template changelog) are
  left alone on purpose; single-slot `(DEV1 : SHARED)` labels are rewritten.

Command slots are cleaned up the same way:
- Unused command blocks were deleted but still referenced — the HOLD composite
  disabled all ten, each command's SFC re-enabled them, and MONITOR tested every one.
  Generating a 2-command EM left 112 references to blocks that were not in the file.
- The MONITOR function block pointed at the template's original composite name after
  that composite had been renamed, so it referenced a definition not present in the
  output. Now renamed together, as COMMAND and ACQ_REL already were.

- The SFC branches for unused command slots are now cut out of the logic rather than
  left testing the stock library set. A 2-command CMD EM's HOLD sequence goes from 12
  steps and 22 transitions to 4 and 6. A branch is only removed when every route into
  it is dead, so nothing reachable is ever dropped, and conditionals the pruning
  empties are collapsed with it.
- No reference to a stock named set survives anywhere in a generated EM.

Found by importing generated EMs into a real DeltaV 15.0 — all three parsed and
round-tripped cleanly and still failed to import:
- Composite names over DeltaV's 16-character limit were silently abbreviated while
  the EM kept referencing the full name, so the module class would not import at all.
  Names are now built inside the limit and de-duplicated.
- The generated named set was written after the composites that use it, so every
  expression logged "unresolved enumeration reference". It is now emitted first.
- Pruning a trimmed device from a flat boolean chain took the statement terminator
  with it, leaving a dangling `AND` and a syntax error. A prune that would leave an
  expression malformed is now refused rather than shipped.

Two additions that make the tool say what it did and what it needs:
- **The Commands list now shows the composite each command will produce.** DeltaV caps
  item names at 16 characters, so "Transfer" on a long EM name becomes
  `TRANSFER_TST_CMD`. The generator shortens names itself now (it has to), and the
  summary line calls out which ones were shortened along with the resulting class and
  named-set names.
- **Overview ▸ Dependencies…** lists what the target database must already contain —
  composites, device classes and named sets — before you attempt an import. DeltaV
  only reports these one failure at a time, and each one cascades into whatever
  referenced it, so the real cause is usually well above the reported error. Works on
  imported documents as well as generated drafts.

Parameter CSV import fixed — it depended on the file's byte count:
- Loading tried UTF-16-LE first and fell back on `UnicodeDecodeError`, but UTF-16-LE
  decodes *any* even-length byte sequence without raising. A UTF-8 CSV whose byte
  count happened to be even decoded into mojibake, matched no columns, and imported
  **nothing at all** — si

P&ID Reader.notes:
# v8 — Far better tag reading

Measured against a hand-checked list of what is actually drawn on a real sheet, this
release finds **29 of 39 tags character-perfect where v7 found 11**, and 4 out of 5
of the tags it reports are now right (v7: fewer than half). It also reads line
numbers, which v7 missed entirely.

- **Pipe spec boxes are no longer reported as equipment.** Every line carries a
  little box with the pipe size over a spec code ("1"" over "B11F"), and those were
  being read as tags — "B11F" became a blower, "C12" a compressor. On one drawing
  that was 56 of the 88 tags found. Serial numbers copied out of notes went the
  same way.
- **Real tags are no longer thrown away.** The reader often sees a tag's dash as an
  underscore, and anything that didn't match the expected pattern was silently
  dropped — which is why no real pump, heat exchanger or line number was appearing.
- **Instrument bubbles are read on their own.** Previously the two lines inside a
  bubble were picked out of a page-wide scan, so a tag could come out as "TE-162"
  with its loop number cut off, depending on where the scan happened to divide the
  sheet. Each bubble is now read individually.
- **The drawing corrects its own loop numbers.** Every loop on a sheet shares an
  area number, repeated in the line numbers and the off-page references. Where that
  got clipped ("TE-2-012" instead of "TE-162-012"), it is restored — and never
  silently: a corrected tag keeps what was originally read and is flagged for review.
- **Loops come out whole.** Those clipped numbers used to split one control loop
  into three or four fragments. A temperature loop that came out as scattered pieces
  now appears complete, with its element, thermowell, transmitter, controller and
  control valve together.
- **Grid references and connectivity work on large sheets.** Border detection failed
  on these drawings, and because the grid is read from the margins outside that
  border, every tag came back with no grid cell. Fixed: grid coordinates are now
  filled in, and connectivity went from 1 connection to over 100.
- **New: a tag register across a drawing set.** Processing a folder now also writes
  `_tag_register.csv` — every tag, how many sheets it appears on, and any similar
  readings worth a second look. Deliberately a report, not an auto-correct: tags are
  numbered in sequence, so neighbouring tags look almost identical and "fixing" them
  automatically would quietly destroy correct data.
- Faster: about a third of the previous image-scanning work per drawing.

# v7 — Large-format drawings

Large sheets (ANSI-D and bigger) failed outright. Two separate size limits, both fixed:

- **Processing crashed immediately on D-size and larger drawings.** At 600 DPI a
  36"x24" sheet renders to 311 megapixels, past the image library's built-in
  safety cap, so the run stopped before it started. The cap now scales with real
  drawing sizes.
- **Bigger sheets then found no tags at all.** Instrument-bubble detection asked
  for one ~864 MB block of memory in a single piece and gave up when it couldn't
  get it, silently emptying the whole extraction — the drawing finished with zero
  tags. Detection now works in tiles, so memory stays flat no matter how large the
  sheet is.

Verified on a 21600 x 14400 drawing: previously a crash, then 0 tags; now 50 tags
extracted and typed, with the full report set written.

Op2Live.notes:
# v29
- **The Source / Value picker actually has the dynamo variables in it.** It
  looked in the studied dynamo class first and fell back to the rule's own
  variables only if that came back empty — but a *class* rule usually has no
  variables of its own (they live on its variants), and the class JSON is
  missing whenever the project was moved or the study was never re-run. Either
  gap produced an empty combo, which on screen is indistinguishable from a plain
  text box. All three sources are now unioned — the studied class, the rule, and
  its variant rules — and variables are listed separately from DeltaV source
  paths under headings rather than run together. When the cell is still empty
  the list opens on click instead of waiting for a double-click; when there is
  genuinely nothing to offer the pane says so, and says to re-run Phase 5,
  rather than showing a blank box.
- **Assigning a GEM to a class now reaches its variants.** They were left with
  no GEM at all — which is not cosmetic: the XSLT build skips any active rule
  whose `Gem` is None, so those instances silently converted inline instead of
  as the GEM. The class and its variants are now assigned together in one
  undoable step, each variant auto-bound against its *own* variables, and
  clearing the class clears the variants that were only carrying its GEM.
- **⚡ Auto-map was doing the work and then throwing it away.** It mutated the
  rule in place but never marked it changed, so the auto-save saw nothing to
  write and the bindings were gone on close. It now goes through the undo stack
  like every other edit, and reports what it did: which properties it bound to
  which variable, which module references it hard-coded, and which are still
  unmapped because nothing matched. Finding nothing is the normal outcome — it
  already runs when the dialog opens — and it now says that instead of looking
  dead.
- **Configure… says what it will configure.** It sat greyed out until a row was
  selected and explained neither state. The first property is now selected
  automatically, the button carries the property's name, and after the dialog
  closes the pane confirms what the property became.
- **The GEM picker can be ranked by match %.** Alphabetical order meant scanning
  a couple of hundred names by hand. An *Order* control now ranks every GEM in
  the enabled libraries by how well its DeltaV references line up with this
  dynamo's — the same structural score the "Why this match" panel explains —
  with the percentage shown against each name. The first ranking reads every GEM
  file and its sub-GEMs; after that it is instant.

# v28
- **Tag display groups no longer multiply.** A holder graphic was getting one
  display for every `.tgd` on the system rather than the ones actually loaded
  into it — on a real plant that meant 5,914 displays where 675 were used, and
  `ROOM_DETAIL_1339`, which is used once, produced 265 copies. The binding is
  now read from the project's own VBA (`OpenTGDPicture "ROOM_DETAIL_3.grf", , 20,
  20, PicPath & "\RS_PU_DF152.TGD"`), which states outright which group loads
  into which picture. Matching on token names is kept only for pictures whose
  call-up computes the picture name at runtime, and anything it matches that no
  call-up mentions is now listed in the conversion log instead of silently
  becoming a display. This also *finds* displays the old rule missed: four
  holders were producing none at all.
- **Tag-group displays are collapsed, not enumerated.** Where a picture's tag
  groups differ in only a few tags — most rows are the same `AI_ENG_Holder`
  placeholders on every instance — they now become ONE contextual display driven
  by up to four contexts, opened once per group. Groups that genuinely vary too
  widely are still expanded, and a set that is mostly uniform with a few odd
  members is split rather than abandoned: 269 room details became 3 displays.

# Patina v3

- **Fixed: Batch (and single decompiles) timing out on large binaries.** A
  binary containing one giant basic block — common in obfuscated code, huge
  compiler-generated dispatch routines, or a misidentified code/data region —
  could spin for many minutes in the IR optimizer, blow past the per-target
  batch timeout, and be killed with *no output at all*. The within-block
  inline/dead-code pass was super-linear in the block's size; it's now bounded so
  a single pathological block can no longer stall a run. Such blocks still
  decompile (in the existing flat "fast mode" view) instead of being dropped.
  Example: a 5 MB bridge binary that never finished now completes in ~30s, and a
  whole folder of them decompiles with zero timeouts.

# Patina v2

- **Fixed: Decompile and Batch did nothing but reopen the window.** Clicking
  Decompile (or Batch, or Auto-fix) relaunched the Patina window instead of
  running the decompiler, because the shipped build looked for a separate
  `patina.exe` next to itself and — on Windows' case-insensitive filesystem —
  matched its own `Patina.exe`. Patina is now a single self-contained binary:
  the same exe is both the GUI and the decompiler it runs, so Decompile/Batch/
  Auto-fix work in the installed build.

# Patina v1

- First release inside the CornerBench suite (Reverse Engineering category).
- Decompiles Windows PE and Linux ELF binaries to readable C via an x86
  disassembler (iced-x86) and a custom IR.
- Function navigation with cross-references.

_Edit this when you bump the version; the launcher shows it as "What's new"
after an in-place update._

# LiveTools v3

A big one. The headline: **the canvas now draws what Live draws.**

## Rendering finally resolves across files

A Live display isn't self-contained — its GEM classes, standard-value colours and
colour tables are the *content of other .ahc files*, usually in other folders.
LiveTools only ever looked in the one "Library folder" box, which was empty by
default. The result: every GEM drew as a grey placeholder tile, and every library
colour was **quietly guessed** by keyword-matching the reference's name. A picture
that was confidently wrong, with nothing to tell you so.

- The renderer now resolves against **every file in your inventory** — add your
  displays *and* your library folders and GEMs expand, with their real colours.
- **GEM instance overrides are applied.** A GEM was previously drawn in its class's
  default colours, ignoring everything the instance changed.
- **Colour tables resolve** to the branch Live takes when no rule matches.
- **Anything still unresolved is reported**, in the status bar, with a tooltip
  listing each reference — including any colour it had to guess. No more silent
  invention.

## Will Graphics Studio actually accept this? — new Import Preflight

A new first tab under **Library** that finds the defects that make a Live import
*fail*, and shows you the exact error Graphics Studio will throw:

- duplicate object names (rejects the **entire display**, not just the object)
- invalid `BooleanCustomPropertyDef` / `NumberCustomPropertyDef` element names
- empty or below-minimum `<Value/>` on int/enum properties
- a colour-returning function bound to a boolean property
- a `String`-typed standard value bound to a localized-string property

Run it before you hand a bundle over.

## Find & Replace you can trust

- **Regex capture groups now work.** `\1` used to be inserted *literally* — regex
  mode was effectively find-only.
- **XML-aware by default.** Edits the parsed document, not raw text, so a broad rule
  can no longer rewrite a tag name, a GUID, or the schema version. Choose what may be
  edited (captions / tags / references / values / names); object names are off by
  default. Untick "XML-aware" for the old raw-text behaviour.
- **It tells you what it *didn't* change.** A new **Skipped** tab lists every match the
  safety gate refused, and why.
- Preview now matches the apply exactly, validation says *what* is wrong instead of
  counting, and you can export a full change-audit CSV.

## Cross-file safety

- **Rename a library item properly** — it moves the file, fixes its name and path,
  and rewrites every reference to it across the project, in one operation.
- **Broken Overrides** report: find GEM overrides that no longer point at anything
  (the breakage a class-side rename causes in every display that uses it) — and
  **repair** the ones that can be unambiguously rebound.
- The editor now **refuses a save that would break other files**, and tells you which.

## Safer, faster, interruptible

- **Every write is atomic and backed up.** A crash mid-save can no longer truncate an
  .ahc, and the original is copied aside before it's overwritten. Saving an unchanged
  file is now a true no-op instead of rewriting its first line.
- **Analyze is ~2.6× faster**, and **Cancel actually works** — on Analyze, on Build,
  on Find & Replace, and on reading a DeltaV backup.
- **One shared file list** across the tabs. Add your project once, not seven times.
- **Translations import to the right string.** Import used to match rows by *position*,
  so adding or deleting any translatable object silently shifted every subsequent
  translation onto the wrong string.
- **SVG export** (vector, crisp at any size) alongside PNG.
- A **headless command line** for CI: `livetools preflight <folder>` exits non-zero if
  a bundle won't import. Also `overrides`, `refs`, `rename`, `fr`, `strings`.

# v8

# v7

## v6

- **Export any table to CSV.** The Discover, Device Explorer and Device Parameters
  tabs each gained an *Export to CSV* button. It writes the table exactly as shown
  — the visible columns, in order, with their heading text — to a CSV file you pick,
  so a discovered-device list, an object-model scan or a full parameter dump can go
  straight into a spreadsheet or a commissioning record. Output is UTF-8 with a BOM
  so Excel opens it without a mojibake prompt.

## v5

- **Probe now prefers the DPI object and reads cleanly on PowerFlex 520-series
  drives.** Validated against a real PowerFlex 525:
  - *Auto* now uses the DPI Parameter Object (0x93) when the device answers a full
    record — it returns name, units, min/max and scaling in one read (e.g.
    parameter 1 → name "Output Freq", units "Hz").
  - The standard Parameter Object (0x0F) fallback was hardened for the PF525's
    quirks: it recovers the parameter name when the drive returns it in the units
    attribute, and **infers the value type from its byte length** when the drive
    reports a non-standard type code — so values show as numbers instead of raw hex.
- Enumeration no longer depends on a working parameter-count read (walks until the
  device stops answering), and the object scan reports parameter-count correctly.

## v4

- **Device introspection — no PDF/EDS needed for most devices.** New *Device
  Explorer* tab plus a *Probe device* button on the parameters tab. The tool now
  asks the device to describe itself:
  - **Identity** — reads the Identity Object (0x01) for product name, revision,
    vendor/type/code, serial.
  - **Self-describing parameters** — walks the DPI Parameter Object (0x93) or the
    standard Parameter Object (0x0F) and reads each parameter's name, type, units,
    min/max/default and **scaling** straight from the device, so you get a live,
    named parameter list (with engineering-unit values) without an EDS. If an EDS
    *is* loaded it enriches the device data (help text, enum strings).
  - **Object-model scan** — probes the well-known CIP classes and shows which the
    device actually implements.
  - **EDS-off-device** (experimental) — uploads the device's own EDS via the File
    Object (0x37), the way Studio 5000/RSLinx do.
  - **Generic explicit-message poker** — send any service/class/instance/attribute
    and decode the reply, for anything the built-in views don't cover.
- **Fixed a second latent read bug:** responses were parsed from the start of the
  raw reply frame instead of the CIP data offset (byte 44). Values/IP config are now
  extracted correctly, and CIP error statuses are decoded to plain English.

## v3

- **Fixed "no parameters could be read" on drives/adapters.** Explicit-message
  reads and writes were being wrapped in an Unconnected_Send routed across a
  backplane to "slot 0" — correct for a ControlLogix chassis, but a standalone
  EtherNet/IP device (PowerFlex drive, EtherNet/IP adapter) has no backplane and
  rejects that route, so every read failed. The tool now sends bare UCMM explicit
  messages directly to the device, the way RSLogix and the drive AOP do.
- **Added the DPI Parameter Object (class 0x93)** used by PowerFlex 520-series
  drives (single read via attr 9; write to NVS via attr 9 or RAM-only via attr 10),
  alongside the generic Parameter Object (0x0F). The Device Parameters tab now has
  a **Parameter object** selector (Auto / DPI 0x93 / Standard 0x0F, default Auto,
  which tries DPI then falls back to 0x0F) and a **Write to** selector (NVS
  permanent / RAM-only temporary).

## v2

- Fixed a startup crash caused by the shared Allen-Bradley EDS library being missing from the packaged build. EDS-based parameter lookup and the tool as a whole now launch correctly.

OperateTools.notes:
# v21
- **New: Repair is its own tab, and no longer needs a find/replace.** Fixing graphics an older version
  damaged used to be a button at the foot of Find & Replace — a screen whose whole purpose is entering a
  replacement rule. It read as though you had to invent an edit before you could fix anything, which is
  the opposite of what you want when the job is "leave this graphic alone except for what is broken".
  It now has its own tab, and it changes nothing but the faults it finds.
- **New: "Scan" tells you which graphics are affected without writing anything.** It reads every picture
  in the inventory and lists, per file, exactly what is wrong — no output folder needed, no files
  touched. Healthy files collapse under a count and unreadable ones are listed separately, so a whole
  project can be surveyed before you decide anything. Repair then writes only the files that are
  actually broken, under the usual choice of an output folder or in-place with a backup, and re-running
  is safe.
- **A find & replace now tells you when a graphic carries damage it cannot fix.** Adding, removing or
  retargeting a term rebuilds the expression, and that path already repairs the whole file on the way
  through — so those edits leave a graphic healthier than they found it. A plain rename cannot: it is a
  same-length text patch that never touches the expression's internals, so it used to copy an older
  version's damage straight into the output with nothing said. Given that this damage looks completely
  correct in the drawing and in every listing, nobody would ever have found out. Preview and Apply now
  report which files carry such faults and offer a link to the Repair tab. It is deliberately a report
  and not an automatic fix: quietly turning a rename into a rewrite of parts you did not ask about is
  its own kind of surprise, and the rename itself is perfectly valid.

# v20
- **Fixed: a number written into an expression was stored wrongly, so the term containing it counted as
  zero.** This is the cause of "the added term does nothing", and it explains every report of it. When
  the editor added a term to an expression, any plain number in that term — the `10` in `... * 10`, a
  threshold, a multiplier — was written in a different numeric format from the one the expression
  declared it to be in. iFix read the declared format, found nothing there, and used zero. The number
  showed correctly in the animation dialog and in every listing, the graphic loaded without complaint,
  and the term it belonged to silently evaluated to nothing: `A * 1 + B * 2 + ( A and B ) * 10` returned
  3 instead of 13, and an added alarm term never took effect no matter what its tags did. Numbers are
  now written the way iFix writes them, verified against 454 of them across four graphics iFix produced;
  "Repair expressions" corrects graphics already written this way; and a graphic can no longer be
  written with a number that does not match the value it displays.
- **Fixed: a new tag connection could be filed under the wrong expression.** iFix addresses a connection
  by a pair — which expression on the object, and which token within it — and both halves are stored in
  the connection itself. The editor set the token half correctly but carried the expression half over
  from whichever existing connection it copied. On an object that owns a single animated property the
  two are always the same and nothing showed; on an object animating several properties from the same
  drawing, a term added to one of them could be delivered to another expression's token instead, so the
  added tag drove nothing while every other tag kept working. The expression half is now written from
  the expression that owns the connection, "Repair expressions" corrects graphics already written this
  way, and a graphic can no longer be written with the two disagreeing.
- **A grown expression no longer has two internal marks rewritten.** An earlier build cleared a mark on
  ea

# v13

## v13

- **Descriptions of an Equipment Module work now.** Asking for one used to fail on
  a "context" error: the fact-sheet handed to the model was 88% comment banner —
  every step action was pasted in whole, `(* ===== *)` header and all — so one
  module came to about 12,900 tokens against a window of 8,192. Comments are
  stripped, each action and transition is capped, and transitions are counted at
  all (there was no limit on them). One real module went from 51,578 characters to
  12,794, and what is left is the logic rather than the decoration.
- **State-driven equipment modules are read at all.** The PCSD `_EM_ST*` exports
  are not Structured Text — they are state-driven, and their table is stored a
  different way. Every one of them listed a module and then described nothing,
  reporting only "not found in the parse". They now come through with their
  devices, and the state table is written the way an engineer reads one: what each
  device rests at and where it differs, rather than 32 identical cells per row.
- **A code review no longer times out.** Two faults in the grammar that shapes the
  model's answers: it could pad a reply with whitespace for ever and still be
  valid, and the length limits were enforced in a way that made the model 40 times
  slower per word. Reviewing four files went from failing after five minutes to
  finishing in eleven seconds. Drafting a whole FAT plan's test steps went from not
  finishing at all to two and a half minutes.
- **"Draft the logic tests" no longer demands a template.** The template only ever
  supplied the cover, revision history and contents of your house FAT plan — never
  the tests. Leave it blank and you get the same plan in a plain document to paste
  under your own front matter; supply one and its front matter is kept exactly as
  it was.
- **The word in the top-left corner tells the truth.** It always read "offline",
  which was meant as the claim that nothing leaves your machine, and looked like a
  warning that something was disconnected. It now says what the local model is
  doing — "starting the model…" while it loads, which takes the best part of a
  minute and nothing used to say so.
- **The requirements document reads the control logic.** A control narrative full
  of interlocks and rules produced a document that said "There is no custom logic
  associated with this system", because nothing ever looked for any. It now reads
  the narrative's systems, its rules, its interlocks and its alarms — and writes
  one section per vessel instead of one section named after the document.
- **An I/O list that is a picture is checked against itself.** Reading one is
  near-perfect at the grid and imperfect at the characters, and a wrong character
  in a tag invents a device. Tags are now repaired from the narrative's own words
  and from loop numbers that appear nowhere else in the table; anything that cannot
  be repaired is reported rather than guessed at, and every correction is listed as
  an open item.
- **Looking things up in a manual reads properly.** Both the fault-code and the
  parameter lookups wrote "Read from in “Appendix B”" on every answer for a
  document without page numbers, which is most of them.
- **A run that is stopped for taking too long says why.** On a machine where the
  model runs mostly on the processor it ended with "TimeoutError: timed out" and
  nothing else. It now explains what happened and what to try, and the limit can be
  raised for a slow machine.
- **Smaller things:** the module list is no longer capped at 400 with advice to
  "raise the cap" and nothing to raise; a generated test file that does not run is
  no longer saved as though it did; explaining an empty file no longer waits on the
  model to be told it is empty; a pathway that names a template or reference it does
  not have is now reported instead of silently doing without.

# v5

- **Push, Pull and Deploy agent now work on nodes that refuse admin file sharing.** They were
  wired straight to `\\host\C$`, so on a hardened station — most of a real DeltaV fleet — they
  simply failed, even though the Screen tab could drive that same node perfectly. They now take

- **A node you can see is now a node you can copy files to.** The last route needs nothing
  installed on the target at all: the file rides the Remote Desktop connection and the node is
  asked to hash what it received, so a transfer either verifies or fails — it never half-lands
  quietly.

  why something that worked on one station fails on the next.

DvVMManager.notes:
# v15

- **Operations now work on a node that allows nothing but Remote Desktop.** Until now every
  operation needed a way to copy a file to the node — admin file sharing or WinRM — because the
  small helper the tool drives the screen with had to get there somehow. A station that offers
  neither could be watched and never automated. The tool can now deliver that helper through the
  Remote Desktop session itself, so a node you can connect to is a node you can run operations on.
- **The transfer is checked, not assumed.** The file is sent in pieces and the node is asked to
  hash what it received; the operation only continues if that matches. If a station allows the
  clipboard only *into* the session — some are configured that way deliberately — the tool has
  the node compare the hash itself and report the verdict, so the check still happens.
- **A dropped session no longer loses the transfer.** Some stations disconnect a session out from
  under whatever is running. Each piece is now sent in a way that is safe to repeat, an
  interrupted transfer restarts rather than corrupting what was already sent, and a file that is
  already on the node with the right contents is not sent again.
- **Fixed: a reconnect could silently empty the clipboard.** If the session dropped between the
  tool putting something on the clipboard and the node reading it, the node read *nothing* — with
  no error shown anywhere. The clipboard now survives a reconnect.

# v14

- **Fixed: Update license failed on a node whose licence dongle wasn't attached, and blamed the
  wrong thing.** On a virtual station the dongle usually isn't plugged into the machine — it sits
  in a SEH dongle server on the network and the station claims it over IP. When the service that
  does the claiming is stopped, Emerson's SID_Update opens with every field blank and the tool
  reported "SID_Update didn't show a System ID", which reads as though the tool or your
  credentials were at fault. Nothing was: the node simply had no licence key.
- **The tool now attaches the dongle for you.** Before it opens SID_Update it checks whether a
  protection key is present, and if the SEH network-USB service is stopped it starts it and waits
  for the key — a few seconds, and the operation carries on normally. It only ever connects the
  port the station was already configured to use; it never takes a dongle from another station.
- **When there really is no key, the message says so in SID_Update's own words** — including its
  "No Protection Key" reading and the reason from its Results list — and tells you to activate the
  station's port in SEH UTN Manager. Previously all of that was read off the screen and discarded.

# v13

- **Fixed: updating a licence failed on some nodes with "SID_Update did not verify the update".**
  The update code was never reaching the box. On these stations the keyboard and mouse we
  synthesise are silently ignored — the click and the paste both report success and nothing
  arrives — while the same node answers everything else we ask it. So the tool filled in
  nothing, pressed Update, and reported the tool's complaint rather than the real problem. The
  code is now put into the field the same way the buttons are pressed, which these nodes do
  accept. Verified on a live station: the code goes in and is read back out of the box.
- **The tool now proves the code is in the box before it presses Update — always.** That check
  existed but only ran in a mode nobody uses. If the code cannot be entered, the operation stops
  and says so, and states plainly that the dongle was not written, instead of pressing a button
  on an empty field and leaving you to guess.
- **When SID_Update says its box was empty, the message says that** rather than implying the
  renewal code was rejected. Those are different faults and were being reported the same way.
- **A failed code entry now records the dialog it was looking at**, so the next occurrence can be
  diagnosed from the

SkillExplorer.notes:
# v6

- **The bundled remote server can now get exact output from a node that allows only Remote
  Desktop.** It previously had one option on such a station — reading the screen — which is fine
  for a yes/no answer but unreliable for values: it has read a version number `10.0.20348` as
  `18.8.28348`. There is now a route that returns the literal text instead, needing no more from

# v5

Note on v4: it was published in the 2026-07-24 suite release without being
rebuilt, so the live v4 download is the v3 binary under a v4 label. Everything
below is what v4 was supposed to contain, plus the graphics-server rename —
this is the first build that actually carries any of it.

Graphics server can now rename

  first writing tool in the MCP catalog. Preview every change first — each one
  showing the graphic, the object, the old and new text, and whether it will be
  edited, skipped or left alone as a protected name — then apply.
- **Your originals are never touched.** Edited copies are written into a folder

SuperComms.notes:
# SuperComms release notes

## v1

First cut: eleven protocols, client and server, behind a grid-first window — plus
the CLI, which stays a first-class way to drive it.

### Connections that need more than an address

Every protocol was audited against one question: *what does connecting to a real
one require, and can you supply it?* Six answers were no.

* **OPC UA had no username/password path at all.** `Credentials` was
  certificate-only and `open_session` never called `set_user`, so a server offering
  `Basic256Sha256 Sign [UserName]` — which is every DeltaV `DvOpcUaServer` — could be
  diagnosed and not connected to. Now: username, password, client certificate with a
  **Generate** button, and channel policy/mode. UA keeps channel security and user
  identity separate and a DeltaV server wants both, so supplying one is checked for
  and explained up front rather than failing with a status code naming neither.
* **EtherNet/IP had no processor slot.** pylogix defaults to 0; a ControlLogix has
  the CPU wherever the drawing put it, and the wrong slot returns an **empty tag
  list and no error**. Slot, Micro800, port and timeout are now driver parameters,
  and all PLC construction goes through one place so a knob cannot be applied in
  some paths and not others.
* **MQTT had no TLS**, while the port hint said "8883 for TLS" — describing
  something that did not exist. Now implemented with CA bundle and client
  certificate, and a certificate failure is reported separately from a dead broker.
* **REST offered a "client certificate" auth mode with nowhere to put the file.**
* **SOAP's WS-Security layer was unreachable** from the form, as was SOAP 1.2 and
  WS-Addressing — the WCF defaults.
* **SQL could not declare write statements**, so its points were silently read-only.

Two bugs fell out of the same sweep. The SQL page assembled an ODBC connection
string at *form-build* time, which needs pyodbc — so on a machine without it the
wizard raised on a Next button before anything had been dialled; the driver now
builds it at connect time, which also keeps the password a named field instead of
buried in an opaque string where name-based redaction cannot see it. And OPC UA with
a generated certificate would have failed anyway: the wizard never passed the
ApplicationUri, which must equal the certificate's SAN URI or the server rejects with
`BadCertificateUriInvalid`.

Removed rather than added: **NTLM is no longer offered for push streams.** That
client applies auth as a header on the opening request and NTLM is a multi-leg
handshake, so the option was a control that silently did nothing.

`tests/test_gui_kinds.py` now checks both directions mechanically — no field the
form collects may be rejected by its driver, and no driver option may be unreachable
from the form.

### Honest about OPC-DA

The bridge activates by COM locally and takes no host — its own error says "not
registered on this **machine**". So classic OPC is **local only**, stated plainly
with OPC UA named as the way to reach another node. The bridge also has a
`list-servers` command nobody had wrapped: the ProgID is now a **discovered list**
rather than free text, because a ProgID is not guessable and a wrong one reports
"not registered", which reads like a broken server rather than a typo.

### The window

Grid-first, in the suite's frameless dark chrome. The live values are the largest
thing on screen and everything else is arranged around them: the connections tree
says what we are talking to, the inspector underneath says what actually crossed the
wire.

* **The quality column is a named column**, not a colour hint. Every `Quality` member
  has its own colour, and so does *never read* — a grid that shows a blank cell for
  never-read, bad and stale alike throws away the whole point of the vocabulary
  underneath. There is a test that fails if a member ever loses its colour.
* **The wire detail is one click away** because it is the reason the tool exists.

# v1

First release. Consolidates **FMTMaker**, **FMTExport** and **ModExport** into one
tool; all three are retired by this release.

## If you used the old tools, read this

Three of the fixes below change the output you will get. They are all corrections,
but they are not silent.

- **FMTExport read the wrong columns from most real templates.** It took the
  parameter line to be the line after `header`, but `must_exist` sits between the
  two — so on 49 of the 62 Emerson PCSD templates it used the literal text
  `must_exist area` as its column list. If you built a workflow around that
  output, FMTTools will give you different (correct) columns.
- **The `.fmt` and its data file disagreed.** The spec declared a tab separator
  while the data was written as comma-separated CSV, so the pair could not import.
  FMTTools writes the data with whatever separator the `.fmt` declares. A
  comma-separated copy is still available as an explicit "for Excel" option.
- **ModExport exported one module, not one per class.** A `return` inside its
  element loop stopped it at the first module with a plant area.

## New

- All nine FMT directives are read and written — `object_subtype`, `must_exist`
  and `skip_lines` were never emitted before, and the object type was hardcoded to
  `Module`.
- **55 object types**, with their exact `begin_format_defn` tokens taken from
  DeltaV's own export engine — up from the 12 the shipped templates cover.
  `EIOC`, `SIS_Module`, `Logic_Solver`, `Modbus_Port`, `WIOC`, `Process_Cell`,
  `Recipe_Parameter`, `Hart_Device`, `Control_Tag`, `PHYSICAL_DEVICE`,
  `LOGICAL_DEVICE`, `SIGNAL` and the rest are all selectable. Each says whether
  its columns come from a shipped template or from documentation.
- **29 documented column contracts** (365 fields with valid values and
  required-for-import flags) from DeltaV's *Valid field values* tables. Enough to
  produce a correct starter worksheet and a valid specification for an object
  type no shipped template covers — OPC UA, Modbus TCP, EtherNet/IP, IEC 61850
  devices and signals, SIS modules, logic solvers, EIOCs.
- The 62 Emerson PCSD format specifications ship with the tool, usable as
  starting points.
- An **I/O** tab, both directions. Pick an object type, get a starter worksheet
  with exactly the columns it needs, fill it in, and get back the `.fmt` + data
  pair — column matching ignores order, case and padding, and anything that does
  not line up either way is reported rather than dropped silently. Or go the
  other way and read the I/O already in an FHX export (`Card`, `Channel`,
  `Charm_IO`). Large exports are streamed: a 274 MB system export is read
  without loading it whole.
- A **Validate** tab: check a `.fmt` and its data file before importing.
- A headless CLI: `FMTTools.exe cli --help` — including `sheet` and `pair` for the
  I/O round trip.

## Fixed

- `is_a_string_parameter` is derived rather than guessed. The old rule matched
  column names against seven substrings and was 87.4% correct against Emerson's
  own templates; specs built from a real export now agree on every shared column.
- Alarm suppression timeouts: the formatter failed outright on any value that was
  not angle-wrapped, and mis-carried the minutes above 1440 (1500 minutes came out
  as `1:1:1440` rather than `1:1:0`).
- Spare DCC conditions were emitted with an index of 0, which does not exist.
- Carriage returns in expressions were never escaped, so DeltaV's CRLF-separated
  Structured Text left a raw carriage return sitting in the exported row.
- Declared-but-unused DCC conditions are materialised again — FMTExport's tidier
  rewrite had dropped that, so those columns were simply missing from its output.
- Array-indexed parameters are kept on module instances; ModExport dropped them.
- A Library export now explains that its modules are templates with no plant area,
  instead of silently producing nothing.
